questions.title: Character of cardiac muscle fibres
questions.question: Which one of the followings is a character of cardiac muscle fibers?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle fibres are packed with mitochondria (up to 40% of cell volume), reflecting their continuous, fatigue-resistant workload — the opposite of "few mitochondria," which better describes a cell built for brief, anaerobic bursts rather than lifelong rhythmic contraction.
explanations.B: Correct. Intercalated discs are step-like junctions crossing cardiac muscle fibres at the Z-lines, joining one myocyte to the next end to end. Their transverse portion (fascia adherens and desmosomes) mechanically anchors neighbouring cells, while their lateral portion (gap junctions) electrically couples them, letting cardiac muscle act as a functional syncytium. No other listed option is a genuine cardiac-muscle-fibre feature.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle fibres typically have a single, central nucleus (occasionally two), not multiple peripheral nuclei — multiple peripheral nuclei is instead the hallmark of skeletal muscle fibres, which are large multinucleated syncytial cells formed by myoblast fusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle fibres are branching and roughly cylindrical, not spindle-shaped — a spindle shape (tapering at both ends, single central nucleus) is instead characteristic of smooth muscle cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle fibres are terminally differentiated and essentially do not regenerate by mitosis of any kind, satellite-cell-mediated or otherwise; satellite-cell-mediated regeneration is a skeletal muscle property, not a cardiac one, which is why myocardial infarction heals by fibrous scarring rather than muscle regrowth.

questions.learning_objective: Identify intercalated discs as the defining junctional feature of cardiac muscle fibres.

questions.title: Aging pigment in cardiac muscle fibres
questions.question: With advance of age, cardiac muscle fibers shows an increase in which one of followings?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosome content reflects a cell's protein-synthesis activity, not its age; cardiac myocytes do not show a specific age-related rise in ribosome number the way they do with lipofuscin.
explanations.B: Correct. Lipofuscin is a yellowish-brown, autofluorescent lipid-protein pigment that accumulates in long-lived, post-mitotic cells like cardiac myocytes as a byproduct of lysosomal degradation of damaged organelles. Because cardiac muscle essentially never divides, this residue is never diluted by cell turnover and instead builds up steadily across a lifetime, making it a recognised "wear and tear" marker of age in histological sections.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intercalated discs are a structural, junctional feature present throughout life at a roughly constant density; they are not an accumulating age marker the way a pigment residue is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T-tubules are a fixed structural feature of the excitation-contraction coupling apparatus, not a substance that progressively accumulates with age in the way lipofuscin does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Purkinje fibres are a distinct cell population of the conducting system, not a substance or feature whose "amount" within ordinary cardiac muscle fibres increases with age.

questions.learning_objective: State that lipofuscin is the pigment that accumulates in cardiac muscle fibres with advancing age.

questions.title: Characteristic of Purkinje muscle fibres
questions.question: Which one of the followings is a characteristic of purkinje muscle fibers?
questions.subject: cvs

options.E: smaller than ordinary cardiac muscle fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. While Purkinje fibres do have some junctional contacts, the option's phrasing does not capture what specifically distinguishes them from ordinary cardiac muscle on a slide — their pale staining is the classic distinguishing histological feature examiners test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The diad tubular system is a feature of ordinary working cardiac muscle's excitation-contraction apparatus; Purkinje fibres are instead notable for having comparatively few T-tubules and a sparse contractile apparatus, since their job is conduction, not contraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Purkinje fibres contain abundant, not small, quantities of glycogen — glycogen is in fact so dense that it dissolves out during routine tissue processing, leaving the characteristic pale, vacuolated appearance.
explanations.D: Correct. Purkinje fibres are modified cardiac muscle cells of the peripheral conducting system that stain pale because they contain few myofibrils (concentrated peripherally) and abundant glycogen (which dissolves during processing, producing a vacuolated look). This pale staining, together with their larger size, is what lets them be recognised histologically against ordinary, more darkly-staining working myocardium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Purkinje fibres are larger, not smaller, than ordinary cardiac muscle fibres — their greater diameter is part of what supports their high conduction velocity.

questions.learning_objective: State that Purkinje fibres are characteristically pale-staining, distinguishing them from ordinary cardiac muscle.

questions.title: Location of T-tubules in cardiac muscle
questions.question: What is the location of T-tubules in cardiac muscle?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The A-I junction is where T-tubules are located in skeletal muscle, not cardiac muscle — this is a classic distractor built on the skeletal-muscle rule being wrongly applied to cardiac tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The intercalated disc is a distinct cell-to-cell junction at the Z-line, a different structure from the T-tubule, which is an invagination of the sarcolemma running into the fibre's interior, not a junction between cells.
explanations.C: Correct. T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that carry the surface action potential deep into the muscle fibre. In cardiac muscle, they are located at the Z-lines, one per sarcomere. They are also wider in calibre than skeletal muscle's own T-tubules, which instead sit at the A-I junction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The A band is the region of overlapping thick and thin filaments in the sarcomere; it is not where T-tubules open into the fibre in either cardiac or skeletal muscle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The I band is the region containing only thin filaments; T-tubules run near the Z-line at the I band's centre, but the anatomically precise, tested location is the Z-line itself, not the I band as a whole.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the cardiac T-tubule at the Z-line, distinct from skeletal muscle's A-I-junction location.

questions.title: Cardiac muscle tubular system
questions.question: Which one of the followings is true concerning the tubular system in cardiac muscle cells?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: Consists of two terminal cisternae of rough endoplasmic reticulum & one T-tubule
options.B: Consists of one terminal cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum & one T-tubule
options.C: Consists of two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum & one T-tubule
options.D: Consists of one terminal cisterna of rough endoplasmic reticulum & one T-tubule
options.E: Consists of one terminal cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum & one of rough endoplasmic reticulum

explanations.A: Incorrect. This option misnames the organelle (rough endoplasmic reticulum, not sarcoplasmic reticulum) and misstates the count (two cisternae, describing skeletal muscle's triad) — cardiac muscle uses sarcoplasmic reticulum specifically, and only one cisterna per T-tubule.
explanations.B: Correct. Cardiac muscle's sarcoplasmic reticulum is less well developed than skeletal muscle's. Each T-tubule couples with only one terminal cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum. This forms a diad, rather than skeletal muscle's triad of one T-tubule flanked by two cisternae.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Two terminal cisternae" describes skeletal muscle's triad arrangement, not cardiac muscle's diad — cardiac muscle has only one cisterna per T-tubule junction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option correctly gives the single-cisterna count but misnames the organelle: the relevant membrane system is sarcoplasmic reticulum (specialised for calcium storage/release), not rough endoplasmic reticulum (specialised for protein synthesis).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum is not part of the calcium-handling tubular system at all; the diad is formed by one T-tubule and one sarcoplasmic-reticulum cisterna, not by two different reticulum types.

questions.learning_objective: State that cardiac muscle's tubular junction is a diad (one T-tubule plus one sarcoplasmic-reticulum cisterna), not a triad.

questions.title: Structure medial to the femoral artery
questions.question: Which one of the following structures lies immediately medial to the femoral artery at the base of the femoral triangle?
questions.subject: cvs

options.C: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

explanations.A: Correct. At the base of the femoral triangle, the femoral nerve, artery and vein sit in that order from lateral to medial ("NAVEL": Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics). The structure immediately medial to the femoral artery is therefore the femoral vein. Both vessels share the femoral sheath, with the vein enclosed in its own medial compartment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery, not medial to it — it is the most lateral of the three main neurovascular structures at this level and sits outside the femoral sheath entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh runs well lateral to the femoral triangle's vessels, entering the thigh near the anterior superior iliac spine, far from the artery's medial border.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lymph node of Cloquet (Rosenmüller) sits within the femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein — one compartment further medial than the vein itself, not immediately medial to the artery.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring, well medial to the femoral vein and canal; it is not the structure immediately adjacent to the femoral artery.

questions.learning_objective: State the lateral-to-medial order of femoral triangle contents and identify the femoral vein as medial to the artery.

questions.title: Origin of the peroneal artery
questions.question: The peroneal artery is a branch of which of the following arteries?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior tibial artery is a separate terminal branch of the popliteal artery running in the anterior compartment; it does not give off the peroneal artery, which arises from the posterior tibial artery instead.
explanations.B: Correct. The popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the posterior tibial artery. A short distance below its own origin, the posterior tibial artery gives off the peroneal (fibular) artery as its largest branch. This artery runs along the fibula, supplying the lateral and deep posterior compartments of the leg and the fibula's own nutrient artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The popliteal artery gives rise to the anterior and posterior tibial arteries directly, not to the peroneal artery — the peroneal artery is one step further down the branching sequence, from the posterior tibial artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The femoral artery lies proximal to the knee and becomes the popliteal artery; it does not directly give off the peroneal artery, which only arises after two further divisions in the leg.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The profunda femoris artery is a thigh vessel supplying the adductor and hamstring muscles; it has no direct continuity with the leg's peroneal artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the peroneal artery is a branch of the posterior tibial artery.

questions.title: Direction of tricuspid regurgitation
questions.question: A 45-year-old female is admitted to the hospital with swelling (edema) of the lower limbs. Ultrasound examination reveals an incompetent tricuspid valve. Into which area will regurgitation of blood occur in this patient?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pulmonary trunk is downstream of the right ventricle, in the direction of normal forward flow — regurgitation through an incompetent tricuspid valve moves backward, upstream, not further forward into the pulmonary circulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left atrium is on the opposite (systemic, left-heart) side of the circulation from the tricuspid valve, which sits between the right atrium and right ventricle; it cannot receive tricuspid regurgitant flow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ascending aorta is downstream of the left ventricle, entirely unconnected to the right-sided tricuspid valve's own inflow/outflow path.
explanations.D: Correct. The tricuspid valve normally seals the right atrioventricular orifice during ventricular systole so the right ventricle ejects forward into the pulmonary trunk. When it is incompetent, some ventricular blood is instead forced backward into the right atrium — the chamber immediately proximal to the valve — producing systemic venous congestion and the peripheral oedema seen in this patient.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The left ventricle is anatomically and functionally separate from the right-sided tricuspid valve (separated by the interventricular septum); it cannot receive tricuspid regurgitant flow.

questions.learning_objective: State that an incompetent tricuspid valve regurgitates blood into the right atrium.

questions.title: Anatomical site of the SA node
questions.question: A 35-year-old female is admitted to the emergency department because of Cardiac arrhythmia. Where is the mass of specialized conducting tissue that initiates the cardiac cycle located?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: At the junction of the coronary sinus and the right atrium
options.B: At the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium
options.C: At the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium
options.D: Between the left and right atria

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium near the AV node's own region, not where the SA node sits — this location instead approximates the AV node's landmark, not the SA node's.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium at its lower end, well away from the SA node, which sits at the upper end of the crista terminalis near the superior, not inferior, caval opening.
explanations.C: Correct. The sino-atrial (SA) node is the specialised conducting tissue that normally initiates each cardiac cycle. It lies in the wall of the right atrium at the junction where the superior vena cava enters. This site is at the upper end of the crista terminalis, distinct from the AV node's own location in the atrioventricular septum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The interatrial septum, between the left and right atria, is not the SA node's location; the SA node sits laterally in the right atrial wall, not on the septum.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The interventricular septum houses the bundle of His and its branches, not the SA node, which is an atrial (not ventricular) structure.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the SA node at the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium.

questions.title: Posterior wall of the left ventricle
questions.question: The posterior wall of the left ventricle comprises which of the following surfaces of the heart?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: Left 1/3 of the sternocostal surface of the heart
options.B: Left 2/3 of the sternocostal surface of the heart
options.D: Left 1/3 of the diaphragmatic surface of the heart
options.E: Left 2/3 of the diaphagmatic surface of the heart

explanations.A: Incorrect. This describes the left ventricle's own (smaller) contribution to the sternocostal (anterior), not diaphragmatic (posterior/inferior), surface of the heart — the wrong surface entirely for a question about the posterior wall.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left ventricle contributes only its left one-third, not two-thirds, to the sternocostal surface; two-thirds is the fraction it contributes to the diaphragmatic surface instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The base of the heart is formed mainly by the left atrium (posteriorly), not the left ventricle's posterior wall, which instead corresponds to part of the diaphragmatic surface.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The left ventricle contributes two-thirds, not one-third, of the diaphragmatic surface — one-third is instead the right ventricle's own share of that surface.
explanations.E: Correct. The heart's diaphragmatic surface rests on the central tendon of the diaphragm and is formed mainly by the left ventricle. Specifically, the left two-thirds of this diaphragmatic surface belongs to the left ventricle and constitutes its posterior wall. The right one-third belongs to the right ventricle, the reverse of the proportions each ventricle contributes to the heart's sternocostal (anterior) surface.

questions.learning_objective: State that the left ventricle's posterior wall is the left two-thirds of the diaphragmatic surface of the heart.

questions.title: Origin of the anterior interventricular artery
questions.question: The anterior interventricular artery is a branch of which of the following?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right coronary artery gives the posterior (not anterior) interventricular artery, along with the marginal artery — the anterior interventricular artery belongs to the left coronary artery instead.
explanations.B: Correct. The left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus of the ascending aorta. After a short main stem, it divides into two terminal branches. One is the anterior interventricular artery, running the anterior interventricular groove with the great cardiac vein; the other is the circumflex artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The circumflex artery is the anterior interventricular artery's own sibling branch, both arising from the left coronary artery — the circumflex does not itself give rise to the anterior interventricular artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery running along the heart's inferior border, unrelated to the anterior interventricular artery's origin from the left coronary artery.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The right conus artery is an early branch of the right coronary artery supplying the conus arteriosus/infundibulum, not the source of the anterior interventricular artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior interventricular artery is a branch of the left coronary artery.

questions.title: Coronary supply of the SA and AV nodes
questions.question: In most of the population, SA node and AV node are supplied by which of the following?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The left coronary artery mainly supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle and the anterior interventricular septum; in the common right-dominant pattern, it does not supply either conducting-system node.
explanations.B: Correct. In most people, the coronary circulation is right-dominant. The right coronary artery then supplies the whole right side of the heart and, importantly, the whole conducting system. This includes both the SA node and the AV node/bundle, which is why right coronary artery occlusion is a classic cause of nodal arrhythmias.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The circumflex artery supplies the SA and/or AV nodes only in the less common left-dominant circulation pattern, not in most of the population, where the right coronary artery is dominant instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Left marginal artery" is not the standard named branch supplying the nodes; the right coronary artery's own marginal branch supplies the heart's inferior border, not the conducting-system nodes directly.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The anterior interventricular artery supplies the ventricles and anterior septum, not the SA or AV nodes, which instead depend on the right coronary artery (or, less commonly, the circumflex) in most individuals.

questions.learning_objective: State that the right coronary artery supplies the SA and AV nodes in most people.

questions.title: Unpaired branches of the abdominal aorta
questions.question: All the following are unpaired branches of the abdominal aorta EXCEPT
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS an unpaired branch). The coeliac trunk is a midline, unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta supplying foregut derivatives, correctly grouped with the other unpaired vessels the question lists — not the exception being asked for.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS an unpaired branch). The superior mesenteric artery is a midline, unpaired branch supplying midgut derivatives, correctly grouped with the unpaired vessels.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS an unpaired branch). The inferior mesenteric artery is a midline, unpaired branch supplying hindgut derivatives, correctly grouped with the unpaired vessels.
explanations.D: Correct — this is the exception. The gonadal arteries are paired, bilateral branches of the abdominal aorta that supply the paired gonads. This distinguishes them from the coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric and median sacral arteries, which are all midline, unpaired branches. Being paired rather than midline is exactly what the question's "EXCEPT" is asking for.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this IS an unpaired branch). The median sacral artery is the aorta's own midline terminal continuation, an unpaired branch, correctly grouped with the others.

questions.learning_objective: List the abdominal aorta's unpaired branches and identify the gonadal artery as paired, not unpaired.

questions.title: Femoral artery continuation through adductor magnus
questions.question: The femoral artery continues as the popliteal artery through the opening in which of the following muscles?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gracilis is a superficial thigh adductor that does not form any opening for the femoral vessels; the femoral artery does not pass through it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adductor longus forms part of the adductor canal's anterior wall/roof but does not itself have the tendinous opening the femoral artery passes through to reach the popliteal fossa — that opening belongs to adductor magnus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adductor brevis lies deep in the medial thigh and, like adductor longus, does not form the specific opening (adductor hiatus) the femoral artery passes through.
explanations.D: Correct. The femoral artery runs down the adductor canal in the thigh's medial compartment. It then leaves the canal by passing through the adductor hiatus, a gap in adductor magnus's distal tendinous insertion. Beyond this opening it enters the popliteal fossa, where it is renamed the popliteal artery.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Popliteus is a muscle of the popliteal fossa itself, distal to where the femoral artery is renamed; it does not form the opening through which the artery passes to become the popliteal artery.

questions.learning_objective: Name adductor magnus's opening (the adductor hiatus) as the passage where the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery.

questions.title: Muscle separating femoral from profunda vessels
questions.question: The femoral vessels are separated from the profunda vessels by which of the following muscles?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sartorius forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle superiorly and later crosses to the medial thigh, but it is not the muscle separating the femoral vessels from the profunda femoris vessels in the adductor canal region.
explanations.B: Correct. Below the femoral triangle, the femoral vessels run superficially within the adductor canal, where adductor longus forms part of the anterior wall. The profunda femoris artery and vein, having branched off more proximally, instead run their own separate course deep to adductor longus. It is this muscle, therefore, that lies between and separates the two vessel planes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adductor brevis lies deeper still, related more to the profunda vessels' own branches than to separating the femoral from the profunda plane, a role specifically attributed to adductor longus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adductor magnus forms the floor of the adductor canal more distally and the adductor hiatus, a different structural role from adductor longus's vessel-separating position.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Popliteus is located distally in the popliteal fossa, well beyond the femoral triangle/adductor canal region where the femoral-versus-profunda vessel relationship is defined.

questions.learning_objective: State that adductor longus separates the femoral vessels from the profunda femoris vessels.

questions.title: Continuation of the anterior compartment leg artery
questions.question: The artery of the anterior compartment of the leg continues as which of the following arteries?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The medial plantar artery is a terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery in the sole of the foot, not the continuation of the anterior tibial artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral plantar artery is likewise a terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery in the sole, unrelated to the anterior compartment's own artery.
explanations.C: Correct. The anterior tibial artery is the artery of the leg's anterior compartment, running between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus. In front of the ankle joint, midway between the two malleoli, it crosses under the extensor retinaculum. There it is renamed the dorsalis pedis artery, which runs onto the dorsum of the foot.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The peroneal artery is a branch of the posterior tibial artery in the deep posterior compartment, an entirely separate vessel from the anterior tibial artery's own continuation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The circumflex fibular artery is a small branch near the knee, not the anterior tibial artery's terminal continuation at the ankle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior tibial artery continues as the dorsalis pedis artery.

questions.title: Structure posterior to a hand in the oblique sinus
questions.question: If you introduce your hand into the oblique sinus of the pericardium then which of the following lies posterior to your hand?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ascending aorta bounds the transverse sinus, anterior to the great vessels, not the structure posterior to a hand placed in the oblique sinus behind the left atrium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pulmonary trunk likewise bounds the transverse sinus anteriorly; it is not posterior to the oblique sinus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior vena cava bounds the transverse sinus's own right side, not the structure lying posterior to the oblique sinus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The left atrium is anterior to the oblique sinus (the sinus lies directly behind it, bounded by the pericardial reflections around the pulmonary veins and IVC) — the left atrium is what the hand is behind, not what lies posterior to the hand.
explanations.E: Correct. The oblique sinus is a blind recess of the pericardium behind the left atrium, bounded by the pericardial reflections around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava. A hand introduced into it, from below, has the posterior pericardial wall immediately behind it. Beyond that wall, in the posterior mediastinum, lies the descending thoracic aorta, the structure therefore posterior to the hand.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the oblique sinus behind the left atrium and name the descending thoracic aorta as posterior to a hand placed in it.

questions.title: Vessel at risk exposing the posterior interventricular artery
questions.question: A 48-year-old male patient had chronic angina. Coronary angiography revealed nearly total blockage of the posterior interventricular artery. In exposing this artery, which accompanying vessel is most susceptible to injury?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Correct. The right coronary artery's posterior interventricular branch runs the posterior interventricular groove accompanied by the middle cardiac vein. This vein shares the same groove as the artery throughout its course. It is therefore the vessel most at risk when a surgeon exposes or operates on the posterior interventricular artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The great cardiac vein accompanies the anterior interventricular artery in the anterior interventricular groove, not the posterior interventricular artery, so it is not the vessel at risk here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The small cardiac vein runs with the right coronary artery in the right part of the coronary sulcus, a different location from the posterior interventricular groove being exposed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the right atrium from the heart's anterior surface, unrelated to the posterior interventricular groove.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The coronary sinus is the common trunk the cardiac veins drain into, located in the posterior coronary sulcus — it is near but distinct from the posterior interventricular groove itself, where the middle cardiac vein specifically runs alongside the artery being exposed.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the middle cardiac vein as the vessel accompanying, and at surgical risk alongside, the posterior interventricular artery.

questions.title: Cause of the cardiac action potential plateau
questions.question: Which of the following is the cause of the plateau phase in the fast response cardiac action potential?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: Balance between inward K + and outward Na+
options.B: Balance between inward Na + and outward K +
options.C: Balance between inward K + and outward Ca ++
options.D: Balance between inward Ca++ and outward K +

explanations.A: Incorrect. This option reverses the correct ion pairing and direction — potassium does not carry an inward current during the plateau, and sodium's own fast inward current has already inactivated by phase 2.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A Na+/K+ balance describes the ionic basis of phase 0's rapid upstroke and phase 3's repolarisation, not the plateau — by the plateau, fast Na+ channels are already inactivated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This option has the calcium direction backward — Ca2+ flows inward (not outward) during the plateau, through L-type calcium channels, balanced against outward K+ current.
explanations.D: Correct. Phase 2 (the plateau) of the fast-response cardiac action potential is sustained by a balance between two currents. An inward Ca2+ current, through L-type calcium channels, is balanced against an outward K+ current through delayed-rectifier channels. This balance holds the membrane near zero millivolts for an extended period, prolonging contraction.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cardiac action potential plateau is caused by a balance between inward Ca2+ and outward K+ currents.

questions.title: Definition of cardiac rhythmicity
questions.question: Rhythmicity: is the ability of the cardiac muscle to
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Correct. Rhythmicity is the heart's own ability to generate spontaneous, regular impulses. It does not need any external nervous stimulation to do so. This property is myogenic, originating within the heart's own specialised pacemaker tissue rather than being imposed by the autonomic nervous system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Responding to an adequate stimulus describes excitability, a related but distinct property of cardiac muscle from rhythmicity, which is specifically about spontaneous, self-generated impulses rather than responsiveness to an external stimulus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transmitting excitation waves describes conductivity, the property that lets the impulse spread from cell to cell, not rhythmicity's own defining feature of spontaneous impulse generation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Contracting to pump blood describes contractility, the mechanical output of cardiac muscle, distinct from rhythmicity, which concerns impulse generation rather than the contraction itself.

questions.learning_objective: Define rhythmicity as the heart's own ability to beat regularly without external stimulation.

questions.title: Dangerous period of cardiac excitability
questions.question: In which period of cardiac action potential, the excitability is considered dangerous due to increased susceptibility to ventricular fibrillation?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. The absolute refractory period is in fact the safest period — no stimulus, however strong, can excite the cardiac muscle then, so it cannot be the source of a dangerous, fibrillation-triggering stimulus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. During the relative refractory period a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed to excite the muscle, making it less dangerous than the supernormal phase, where even a weak, subthreshold stimulus suffices.
explanations.C: Correct. The supernormal phase of excitability coincides with the last half of repolarisation. During this brief window, even a weak, subthreshold stimulus can excite the cardiac muscle. A stimulus landing during this vulnerable period can trigger a re-entrant arrhythmia, up to and including ventricular fibrillation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Resting period" is not a standard named phase of cardiac excitability in this sequence; the tested dangerous window is specifically the supernormal phase at the tail of repolarisation.

questions.learning_objective: Name the supernormal phase of excitability as the dangerous, vulnerable period for triggering ventricular fibrillation.

questions.title: Ion responsible for autorhythmic cell depolarization
questions.question: Which one of the following ions is responsible for depolarization phase of the auto rhythmic cell action potential?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Na+ influx through fast sodium channels drives depolarization in a working (non-pacemaker) myocyte, but in an autorhythmic cell those fast Na+ channels are largely inactivated at its less negative resting range, so Na+ is not the depolarizing ion there.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chloride movement is not the mechanism driving the depolarization phase of the autorhythmic action potential in standard cardiac physiology teaching for this cell type.
explanations.C: Correct. An autorhythmic (pacemaker) cell never rests at a fixed potential; a slow pacemaker current continuously drifts it toward threshold. Once threshold is reached, its depolarization upstroke is carried by Ca2+ influx through L-type calcium channels, not by fast Na+ channels. Fast Na+ channels stay largely inactivated at the pacemaker cell's less negative resting range, which is why this Ca2+-driven upstroke is slower and smaller in magnitude than a working myocyte's own Na+-driven one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. K+ outflux (efflux) drives repolarization, not depolarization — it moves the membrane potential in the opposite direction from what this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: State that Ca2+ influx through L-type channels drives depolarization of an autorhythmic cell, unlike a working myocyte's Na+-driven upstroke.

questions.title: Factor that increases heart rate
questions.question: Which one of the following factors increases the heart rate?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Correct. Increased venous return distends the right atrium, mechanically stretching the pacemaker cells of the SA node sitting in its wall. This stretch increases SA-node permeability to Ca2+ through L- and T-type channels. The result, the Bainbridge reflex, speeds the pacemaker's own spontaneous depolarisation and raises heart rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Severe hypoxia typically triggers a reflex bradycardia (via chemoreceptor-mediated vagal stimulation) rather than a straightforward rise in heart rate, especially once compensatory sympathetic drive is overwhelmed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypokalemia's effects on cardiac excitability and rhythm are complex and arrhythmogenic, but it is not the mechanism this question is testing for a straightforward heart-rate increase — increased venous return via the Bainbridge reflex is the intended, unambiguous answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation decreases, not increases, heart rate — the opposite effect from what this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: State that increased venous return raises heart rate via the Bainbridge reflex.

questions.title: Factor facilitating conduction between cardiac cells
questions.question: What is the primary factor facilitating the conduction of electrical signals between cardiac cells?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cardiac cells do not rely on neurotransmitter release to conduct the impulse from one myocyte to the next — that mechanism describes synaptic transmission between neurons or at neuromuscular junctions, not direct cell-to-cell cardiac conduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Gap junctions form the lateral portion of each intercalated disc. They are low-resistance channels that let the action potential spread directly from one cardiac myocyte to the next, without any nerve or neurotransmitter. This direct electrical coupling is what makes cardiac muscle behave as a functional electrical syncytium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hormonal regulation can modulate cardiac rate and force over time, but it is not the mechanism by which the electrical signal itself passes from one cardiac cell to its neighbour.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Voltage-gated ion channels generate and shape the action potential within a single cell, but the question asks what lets the signal pass BETWEEN cells — that role belongs to gap junctions.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gap junctions as the structure that lets electrical signals conduct from one cardiac cell to the next.

questions.title: Site of the cardiac conduction delay
questions.question: Which part of the cardiac conduction system is responsible for delaying the electrical impulses to allow complete atrial contraction?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Purkinje fibres are the fastest-conducting part of the system, distributing the impulse rapidly through the ventricles — the opposite role from delaying it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The bundle of His conducts relatively quickly, carrying the impulse from the AV node into the ventricular conducting system; it is not the site of the deliberate delay.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The SA node initiates the impulse but does not itself introduce the delay that separates atrial from ventricular activation — that delay occurs further along the pathway, at the AV node.
explanations.D: Correct. The AV node's conduction is unusually slow compared with the rest of the cardiac conducting system, taking roughly 0.1 second to cross. This deliberately delays the electrical impulse on its way from the atria to the ventricles. The delay allows the atria just enough time to complete their own contraction before the ventricles are electrically activated.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the AV node as the site of the conduction delay that allows complete atrial contraction.

questions.title: Significance of the AV node delay
questions.question: What is the significance of impulse delay in the atrioventricular node (AVN)?
questions.subject: cvs

options.B: Allows sufficient time for complete atrial contraction.
options.D: Protects the atria from high ventricular rhythm.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This states the opposite of the delay's purpose — the AV node delay does not prevent atrial contraction, it allows the atria the time needed to complete their contraction before the ventricles activate.
explanations.B: Correct. The AV node's conduction delay allows the atria sufficient time to finish contracting before the ventricles are electrically activated. This keeps atrial and ventricular contraction sequential rather than simultaneous. Sequencing the two in this way optimises ventricular filling and, through it, stroke volume.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The delay slows, rather than speeds up, the onset of ventricular contraction relative to atrial contraction — its purpose is sequencing, not acceleration.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Protecting the ventricles from an excessively high atrial rate is a separate, rate-limiting/filtering role the AV node can play during atrial arrhythmias, not the delay's normal-rhythm purpose being tested here (which is about sequencing atrial-before-ventricular contraction), and this option also reverses which chamber is being protected from which.

questions.learning_objective: State that the AV node delay allows the atria sufficient time to complete contraction before ventricular activation.

questions.title: Fastest-conducting part of the conducting system
questions.question: Which part of the conducting system has the fastest speed of conduction?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atrial muscle conducts at an intermediate speed, faster than the AV node but well short of the Purkinje system's own high conduction velocity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. AV nodal fibres are in fact the slowest-conducting part of the whole system — the deliberate site of the cardiac conduction delay — the opposite of fastest.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The bundle of His conducts quickly but is still slower than the Purkinje fibre network it feeds into, which achieves the highest conduction velocity of any part of the conducting system.
explanations.D: Correct. Purkinje fibres conduct the cardiac impulse faster than any other part of the conducting system, up to about 4 m/s. This high conduction velocity lets the Purkinje network distribute the impulse almost simultaneously throughout both ventricles. As a result, the ventricular myocardium contracts as a coordinated unit rather than as a slow, spreading wave.

questions.learning_objective: Rank Purkinje fibres as the fastest-conducting part of the cardiac conducting system.

questions.title: Meaning of cardiac contractility
questions.question: What is the meaning of contractility regarding cardiac function?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: The ability of the cardiac muscle to relax effectively.
options.B: The ability of the cardiac muscle to generate force and contract.
options.C: The ability of the cardiac muscle to regulate heart rate.
options.D: The ability of the cardiac muscle to conduct electrical impulses

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ability to relax effectively describes lusitropy (relaxation property), a related but distinct cardiac property from contractility, which concerns force generation during contraction, not relaxation.
explanations.B: Correct. Contractility (inotropy) is the intrinsic ability of cardiac muscle to generate force and contract. It is set by how much calcium reaches the contractile myofilaments, independent of the fibre's own resting length. This is what separates contractility from the Frank-Starling mechanism, where force instead depends on stretch (preload).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Regulating heart rate is chronotropy, a separate cardiac property from contractility, which is specifically about the force/strength of contraction, not the rate of beating.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conducting electrical impulses is conductivity, a distinct property from contractility — conductivity concerns impulse transmission, contractility concerns the mechanical force generated once the impulse arrives.

questions.learning_objective: Define contractility as the ability of cardiac muscle to generate force and contract.

questions.title: Frank-Starling law and diastolic filling
questions.question: According to the Frank-Starling law, what happens to cardiac contractility when the heart fills with more blood during diastole?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. This states the opposite of the Frank-Starling relationship — a rise in diastolic filling (end-diastolic volume) increases, not decreases, the force of the next contraction, within physiological limits.
explanations.B: Incorrect. If contraction force stayed constant regardless of filling, the heart could not automatically match its output to venous return — the whole point of the Frank-Starling mechanism is that force DOES change (rises) with increased filling.
explanations.C: Correct. Per the Frank-Starling law, within physiological limits, a rise in end-diastolic (ventricular filling) volume raises the force of cardiac contraction — greater diastolic fill stretches the sarcomeres closer to their optimal length for cross-bridge formation, so the heart automatically pumps out whatever volume flows in. (Note: strictly, this is a stretch-dependent, length-based mechanism rather than a change in true calcium-availability-based contractility, but the department's own exam key phrases the response as "contractility increases," and that printed key stands.)
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Frank-Starling response is a predictable, graded rise in force with increased filling, not an irregular or unpredictable change.

questions.learning_objective: State that, per the Frank-Starling law, increased diastolic filling raises the force of cardiac contraction.

questions.title: Effect of positive inotropic drugs
questions.question: How do positive inotropic drugs influence cardiac muscle?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is the definition of a NEGATIVE inotropic drug, the opposite of what a positive inotropic drug does — positive inotropes raise, not lower, contractility.
explanations.B: Correct. A positive inotropic agent raises contractility by increasing intracellular calcium availability to the myofilaments. This produces a stronger contraction at any given fibre length. Because the effect does not depend on extra ventricular filling, such drugs raise stroke volume directly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inotropic drugs act on contractility (force of contraction), not directly on rhythmicity (the heart's own spontaneous impulse generation) — a drug's inotropic and chronotropic/rhythm effects are distinct properties.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Similarly, "increase rhythmicity" describes a chronotropic effect, not the inotropic (contractility) effect this question specifically asks about.

questions.learning_objective: State that positive inotropic drugs act by increasing cardiac contractility.

questions.title: Role of vagal stimulation in cardiac function
questions.question: What is the role of the vagus (parasympathetic) nerves in cardiac functions?
questions.subject: cvs

options.C: To increase excitability of cardiac fibers.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increasing heart rate is the sympathetic nervous system's own effect, not the vagus's — the two autonomic branches have opposite chronotropic actions on the heart.
explanations.B: Correct. The vagus (parasympathetic) nerves supply the SA node, AV node and atrial muscle, via postganglionic fibres releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. Acetylcholine hyperpolarises the SA node and slows its rate of spontaneous depolarisation. This lengthens the interval between beats, decreasing heart rate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vagal stimulation does not raise cardiac fibre excitability; if anything, its hyperpolarising action makes the SA node less, not more, readily excitable.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Promoting vasoconstriction is a sympathetic (alpha-adrenergic) vascular effect, not a direct cardiac action of the vagus nerve, whose principal cardiac role is slowing the heart rate.

questions.learning_objective: State that vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation decreases heart rate.

questions.title: Ventricular pressure during isovolumetric contraction
questions.question: What happens to ventricular pressure during the isovolumetric contraction phase?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Correct. During isovolumetric contraction, all four heart valves are closed — the AV valves have just shut, and the semilunar valves have not yet opened. The contracting ventricle therefore cannot eject any blood. All its mechanical work instead goes into rapidly raising ventricular pressure, until it exceeds aortic pressure and forces the semilunar valve open.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pressure rises, not decreases, during this phase — the ventricle is actively contracting against a closed system, which drives pressure up, not down.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pressure changes dramatically during isovolumetric contraction even though volume stays constant — it is volume, not pressure, that remains fixed in this phase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pressure rise during isovolumetric contraction is a smooth, predictable increase driven by ventricular contraction against closed valves, not an irregular fluctuation.

questions.learning_objective: State that ventricular pressure rises rapidly during isovolumetric contraction while volume stays constant.

questions.title: Cause of the atrial pressure a-wave
questions.question: What causes the ascending limb of a-wave in the atrial pressure curve?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ventricular relaxation is associated with the atrial pressure curve's v-wave descent and the isovolumetric relaxation phase, not the a-wave's own ascending limb, which is atrial (not ventricular) in origin.
explanations.B: Correct. The a-wave is the first and largest wave in the atrial pressure curve. It is produced directly by atrial contraction (atrial systole), which raises atrial pressure as the atrium squeezes its contents against the still-closed AV valve. The smaller c-wave and v-wave that follow instead reflect separate, later events in the cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ventricular ejection occurs after the AV valves close and is instead associated with the atrial pressure curve's c-wave (AV valve bulging back into the atrium), not the a-wave.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atrial relaxation would lower, not raise, atrial pressure, so it cannot explain the a-wave's ascending (rising) limb.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the a-wave's ascending limb to atrial contraction.

questions.title: Phase of markedly decreasing ventricular volume
questions.question: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does the ventricular volume markedly decreases?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. During isovolumetric relaxation, all valves are closed and volume is fixed by definition — no blood leaves the ventricle, so volume cannot markedly decrease in this phase.
explanations.B: Correct. Once the semilunar valve opens, the maximum (rapid) ejection phase begins. A large fraction of the stroke volume leaves the ventricle in a short time. Ventricular volume therefore falls sharply during this phase, more than in any other part of the cardiac cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. During the maximum filling phase, blood enters the ventricle from the atrium, so ventricular volume rises, not falls.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atrial systole adds a further, smaller increment to ventricular filling (the atrial "kick"), so ventricular volume rises slightly during this phase too, not decreases.

questions.learning_objective: State that ventricular volume falls sharply during the maximum (rapid) ejection phase.

questions.title: Phase of maximum aortic pressure
questions.question: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does the aortic pressure markedly increases and reaches maximum value?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Correct. During the maximum (rapid) ejection phase, aortic pressure rises alongside the sharp outflow of blood leaving the ventricle. Outflow still exceeds what runs off into the periphery through most of this phase. Aortic pressure therefore keeps climbing and reaches its maximum value at the end of the maximum ejection phase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aortic pressure does not rise during isovolumetric contraction — the aortic valve is still closed at that point, so ventricular contraction has not yet begun to affect aortic pressure at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aortic pressure is instead declining through diastole, which includes the maximum filling phase, as blood runs off into the periphery faster than any inflow from the (closed-valve) ventricle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atrial systole is a diastolic-phase event on the ventricular side and has no direct effect on aortic pressure, which continues its diastolic decline through this period.

questions.learning_objective: State that aortic pressure reaches its peak during the maximum (rapid) ejection phase.

questions.title: Cause of the aortic pressure incisura
questions.question: Incisura in aortic pressure curve is caused by which of the following?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Semilunar valve opening marks the START of ejection, at the beginning of the aortic pressure rise, not the incisura, which instead occurs at the END of ejection when the valve closes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Atrial systole is an atrial-pressure-curve event (producing the a-wave), unrelated in timing or mechanism to the aortic pressure curve's own incisura.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A sudden increase in ventricular filling would be a diastolic, ventricular-side event, not the cause of a notch in the aortic pressure curve, which reflects events at the aortic valve and aortic wall.
explanations.D: Correct. The incisura is caused by sudden closure of the aortic valve, as ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure at the end of ejection. This produces a sharp, brief dip in the aortic pressure curve. It is immediately followed by a small secondary rise, as the elastic wall of the aorta recoils against the now-closed valve.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the aortic pressure curve's incisura to aortic valve closure and elastic recoil of the aorta.

questions.title: Primary determinant of preload
questions.question: Which one of the following factors primarily determines preload?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Correct. Preload is the degree of ventricular wall stretch just before contraction, produced by end-diastolic filling. How much the ventricle fills depends on how much blood flows back to the heart. Venous return is therefore preload's primary determinant.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Afterload is a separate load the ventricle must overcome DURING contraction (determined by vascular resistance), not what determines preload, the filling condition BEFORE contraction begins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Heart rate affects how much time is available for filling (and thus can influence preload indirectly at very high rates), but it is not itself preload's primary determinant — venous return is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stroke volume is an OUTPUT of the heart's pumping action, partly determined by preload itself (via Frank-Starling), not the determinant of preload — the causal direction here runs from venous return to preload to stroke volume, not the reverse.

questions.learning_objective: State that venous return is the primary determinant of preload.

questions.title: Phases when the AV valves remain open
questions.question: During which phases of the cardiac cycle do the atrioventricular valves remain open?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Atrial diastole" as a labelled option here does not correspond to the specific AV-valve-open phase being tested — the AV valves are open through ventricular diastole's filling phases, of which maximum filling is the one this question's key identifies.
explanations.B: Correct. The AV valves open once ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, at the start of ventricular diastole. They then stay open throughout ventricular filling. This includes the most active portion of filling, the maximum (rapid) filling phase, when blood rushes from the atria into the still-relaxing ventricles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. During isovolumetric contraction, the AV valves have just closed (along with the semilunar valves still shut) — this is one of the two phases where all valves are closed, not one where the AV valves are open.
explanations.D: Incorrect. During isovolumetric relaxation, the AV valves have not yet opened (ventricular pressure is still falling, above atrial pressure) and the semilunar valve has just closed — again a phase where all valves are closed, not where the AV valves are open.

questions.learning_objective: State that the AV valves are open throughout the maximum (rapid) filling phase of the cardiac cycle.

questions.title: True statement regarding afterload
questions.question: Which one of the following statements regarding afterload is true?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: Decrease in venous return leads to an increase in afterload.
options.B: Afterload primarily is the volume of blood in ventricles at the end of systole.
options.C: Afterload is determined by the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole.
options.D: Afterload is primarily influenced by systemic vascular resistance and pulmonary vascular resistance.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Venous return determines preload, not afterload — the two are governed by different, largely independent factors (venous return/filling for preload, vascular resistance for afterload), so a change in venous return does not directly translate into a change in afterload.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The volume of blood remaining in the ventricle at the end of systole is end-systolic volume, an OUTCOME influenced by afterload and contractility, not afterload's own definition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole is end-diastolic volume, which determines preload, not afterload — this option describes the wrong load entirely.
explanations.D: Correct. Afterload is the load or pressure that ventricular muscle must overcome during contraction in order to eject blood. It is primarily set by the resistance the ejected blood meets downstream. For the left ventricle this is systemic vascular resistance, and for the right ventricle it is pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.learning_objective: State that afterload is primarily determined by systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.title: Main determinant of venous return
questions.question: What is the main determinant of venous return?
questions.subject: cvs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stroke volume is an output of cardiac pumping, itself partly a consequence of venous return (via preload), not the determinant driving venous return in the first place.
explanations.B: Correct. Venous return is driven by the pressure gradient between the mean systemic filling pressure and right atrial pressure. The mean systemic filling pressure is set mainly by total blood volume and venous tone. Because it is the larger of the two pressures in this gradient and the one that varies most with volume and tone, it is the main determinant of venous return.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cardiac output and venous return are linked (they must equal each other in steady state), but cardiac output is not itself the determinant of venous return — venous return is instead governed upstream by MSFP and right atrial pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myocardial contractility affects how effectively the heart pumps blood forward, which can influence right atrial pressure and thus the venous-return gradient indirectly, but it is not the main, direct determinant of venous return itself.

questions.learning_objective: Name the mean systemic filling pressure as the main determinant of venous return.

questions.title: Definition of cardiac reserve
questions.question: What is cardiac reserve?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: The ability of the heart to increase its output above baseline levels in response to physiological demands.
options.B: The ratio of work output to total chemical energy used to perform the work.
options.C: The volume of blood ejected by the heart with each contraction.
options.D: The forcefulness of cardiac muscle contraction

explanations.A: Correct. Cardiac reserve is the maximum percentage by which cardiac output can rise above its resting baseline. It is drawn on during exercise or other physiological stress. It has two components: heart-rate reserve, up to a maximal rate near 220 minus age, and stroke-volume reserve, raised through increased end-diastolic volume and positive inotropy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ratio of work output to total chemical energy used describes cardiac efficiency, a distinct concept from cardiac reserve, which concerns available output headroom above baseline, not energetic efficiency.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The volume of blood ejected with each contraction is stroke volume, a single measured quantity, not the concept of RESERVE (headroom to increase output), which this question specifically asks about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The forcefulness of cardiac muscle contraction describes contractility, a related but distinct concept from cardiac reserve, which is about the heart's overall capacity to raise output, not the force of an individual contraction.

questions.learning_objective: Define cardiac reserve as the heart's ability to raise output above resting baseline in response to physiological demand.

questions.title: Effect of raised right atrial pressure on venous return
questions.question: Which of the following is a normal response to increase in the right atrial pressure above zero?
questions.subject: cvs

options.A: The cardiac output is suddenly decreased.
options.C: Collapse of the veins entering the chest.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A rise in right atrial pressure produces a gradual, progressive fall in venous return (and, through it, cardiac output) rather than a sudden drop in cardiac output as a direct, immediate response.
explanations.B: Correct. Venous return depends on the pressure gradient between the mean systemic filling pressure and right atrial pressure. As right atrial pressure rises above its normal near-zero level, this gradient narrows. Venous return therefore falls progressively, reaching zero once right atrial pressure reaches about +7 mmHg.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Collapse of the large veins entering the thorax is instead the response to a FALL in right atrial pressure BELOW zero (subatmospheric), not to a rise above zero, which is what this question asks about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Semilunar valve opening is governed by the relationship between ventricular and aortic/pulmonary pressure during systole, unrelated to right atrial pressure's effect on venous return.

questions.learning_objective: State that a rise in right atrial pressure above zero progressively decreases venous return.
